introduction: The Caribbean History School-Based Assessment is a research project on a historical topic of your choice, based on primary and secondary sources. It rewards a clear question, evidence that is used rather than copied, and a judgement of your own. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the exact requirements and marks for your examination session.

tasks.title: Research Question
tasks.explanation: State the question your project will answer and why it is historically significant.

tasks.title: Aims
tasks.explanation: List two or three specific objectives that the research will achieve.

tasks.title: Methods
tasks.explanation: Explain how you will gather evidence: which archives, libraries, newspapers, oral testimonies or interviews.

tasks.title: Sources
tasks.explanation: Present your evidence - extracts, photographs, tables, summaries of interviews - with the source of each item recorded.

tasks.title: Analysis
tasks.explanation: Interpret the evidence: what does it show, whose viewpoint does it represent, and how reliable is it?

tasks.title: Findings
tasks.explanation: State your conclusions, answer your research question, and note what further research would help.

sampleTitle: How did the 1938 labour disturbances in Jamaica change the relationship between workers and the colonial government?

sample.body: This project examines why the 1938 unrest on the Kingston waterfront produced permanent trade unions and political parties, while earlier strikes had not.
sample.tips: Keep the question narrow enough to answer with the sources you can reach.

sample.body: The Moyne Report (1939) states that wages on the waterfront were insufficient for a family to live on. Read against the newspaper reports of the strike, this shows that the commission's evidence confirmed what workers had already said in public - the argument was not only about wages but about who had the right to be heard.
sample.tips: Quote the source briefly, then explain what it shows and how far it can be trusted.

marking: Marks reward a clear research question, evidence drawn from identified sources, analysis rather than narration, awareness of bias and viewpoint, and a supported conclusion. Copied extracts without comment earn little.
checklist: Analysis shows use of evidence, not just narration
Viewpoint and reliability of sources discussed
